utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Ms. D'Ascoli, you are to take the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The next witness is Mr. Emin Kabashi and his evidence relates to paragraph 72(g), 73, and 77 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The witness will be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kabashi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Ms. D'Ascoli has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I am Emin Kabashi.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And when and where were you born, Mr. Kabashi?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I was born in 1949 in a village in the Dukagjini Plain, Rahovec municipality, I live in Fushe Kosove of Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. So you said that you currently living in Fushe Kosove; right?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thanks. Mr. Kabashi, I understand that you have a Ph.D. degree from the University of Pristina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And in which field is your Ph.D.?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Philological studies.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thanks. Which is your current occupation, Mr. Kabashi?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: My present occupation is scientific advisor in the Albanological Institute of Prishtina. This is the highest academic degree.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 24th of April, 1999, did you provide a statement to a representative to the office of the Prosecutor about events that you had witnessed in Kosovo Polje and in Pristina in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And have you recently had the opportunity to review your written statement?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you satisfied that the information contained in it is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, it is very accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender the 65 ter number 02250 which is the witness statement of Mr. Kabashi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00424, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, did you also testify about the same events before this Tribunal in August 2006 in the Milutinovic et al case?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I did testify. I also testified in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you recently had the opportunity to review the transcript of your testimony in the Milutinovic et al case?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I listened to it, and I read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you were asked the same questions that you were asked during your testimony in the Milutinovic et al case, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Almost the same answers. Maybe the wording might change, but the answer would be the same more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender the 65 ter number 05195 into evidence, and this is the transcript of Mr. Kabashi's testimony in the Milutinovic et al case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00425, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I will now proceed to read the summary of this witness's evidence. The witness describes the actions of Serbian forces in Kosovo Polje, or Fushe Kosove, and in Pristina in March 1999 and the events which led to the departure of a large number of people from the Pristina municipality. On 25 March 1999 the witness observed Serb forces, police, and armed civilians in the street near his house. After an explosive device was thrown into his house that day, the witness spent the night in the loft of a three-storey house, from where he was able to see Albanian houses and shops being burned. The following day he fled to Pristina with some members of his family, where he stayed for some days in different neighbourhoods and in different houses. He was then expelled by the Serbian army and police and eventually directed to the railway station. The witness stayed there for three days and three nights and describes the conditions at the train station. The witness was then forced on to a cargo train to Djeneral Jankovic, and once there he was ordered to walk to the Macedonian border. He was eventually transferred to Albania by bus. And this is the end of the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, now I would like to move to your statement and to ask you some questions about the events you described there; but before that can I just ask you: Were you at any time a member, and in particular March 1999, a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And as you explained already in your testimony in the Milutinovic case, you were part of a logistic unit that dealt with providing material supplies, food, medicine, et cetera to other members; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'll be moving to March 1999. Where were you living at the time, in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Until the 24th of March I lived in my house in Fushe Kosove. When I was not at my house, I lived in various places depending on what work I was doing on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thanks. But in March 1999 you were in Fushe Kosove. And is Fushe Kosove --

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thanks. Is the Serbian name of Fushe Kosove Kosovo Polje; right?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Do you have you any children; and if yes, how many?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, three children, one boy and two girls.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's move to the 25th of March, 1999. At page 2, paragraph 3 of your statement - and this is both the English and B/C/S version - you describe how you left your house following an explosive and a volley of automatic gun-fire, and you say you carried your mother in the cellar of a friend's house where there were more than 50 people. I would like to ask you who those people were and what their ethnicity was, if you know.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: My family members, my mother and all the other people who were in that cellar were Albanians, my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And do you know why they were there?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: They were also forced to leave their homes because of the danger posed to them by the military Serb forces and police forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's now move on to the day that you left Kosovo Polje and went to Pristina. That was the 26th of March, 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And do you know how far is Kosovo Polje from Pristina approximately?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Approximately 7 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, at pages 3 to 4 of your statement you say that you first stayed in the Dragodan neighbourhood of Pristina and then in the Vranjevc neighbourhood. I'm going to show you a map.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Could I please have on the screen the 65 ter number 00013. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, do you recognise what's depicted in this map?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you see in this map the neighbourhoods where you stayed?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, although --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you name them?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: This is Dragodan --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: This is a map of -- this is a map of Pristina; correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, it is a map of Prishtina, although some parts are missing here. So this is Dragodan. North of Dragodan, somewhere here, although it doesn't say Vranjevc, it is the Vranjevc neighbourhood right there.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you mark -- could you put a number 1 close to the Dragodan neighbourhood and a number 2 close to the Vranjevc neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I just did.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this exhibit as marked by the witness and this is the 65 ter number 00013.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, at page --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00426, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, at page 3 of your statement in the last paragraph you mention that when the army and the special police broke into the house of Qemal Avdiu, and this was in the Dragodan neighbourhood of Pristina where you and other people were staying, they ordered you to put your hands up, they separated women and children, and they asked money from you. You also described that ID cards were taken away from the women who were in the room with you. Can you please tell us and specify who confiscated these ID cards from the three women -- from the women?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: In Qemal Avdiu's house, who is a friend of the family, we stayed there for about three days and two nights or vice versa, three nights and two days. In the morning, suddenly the doors were broken in and the police came into the room where I was staying with my family together with my wife, my sister-in-law, my eldest daughter with her child, another woman who had been sheltering there just like us. This woman I didn't know. And after the police came in, they asked us to put our hands up, which we did, and then they separated the women from us. The women were told to go to the corridor, and before they went there, their ID cards were taken and torn and thrown away.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Was it the same forces who took these ID cards? Can you specify exactly who they were? You mentioned the police.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: According to what we had been seeing in Kosova during that time, these were special police forces. Their uniforms were different from the normal police uniform, and some of them who did not have masks on their faces, they had painted faces and they had baseball caps on up to their eyebrows, pulled down up to their eyebrows. We did not have any occasion to see such forces before. We had not had any occasion to face such forces before.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said that those forces eventually took you out of the house and you were taken to the neighbourhood of Vranjevc. At page 4 in paragraph 2 of your statement you refer to approximately 50 people sleeping in one room at Qamil Berisha's house. Can I ask you what was the ethnicity of those people and if you know why they were there?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: When we were forced out of this house, the women were not even allowed to put on their shoes; they had to go out barefoot. And we were directed towards Vranjevc. And while we were walking in that direction, Qamil Berisha recognised us, and he took us into their home -- into his home, and in that house there were about 50 people, all of them were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And do you know why they were there?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: All of them had been expelled from their homes and in order not to sleep outside, to sleep rough, they were able to find a shelter and went there.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thanks. I would like now to move to the morning of the day you were forced to go to the train station. First of all, which train station now we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: It was the Prishtina train station. Prishtina has only got one train station.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thanks. And at page 4, paragraph 4, of your statement you mention a very long column of people on the street. Can you tell me what you observed on your way to the train station that morning.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Those who know Prishtina and the neighbourhood of Vranjevc from where we were forced out that morning, that neighbourhood is in a sort of a valley and we could hear shelling and fire-arms. We were told and ordered to go towards town, down-town. On the asphalted road, the column was divided into two parts by a tank on the bridge and one part was told to go towards the Medrese while the other part of the column was ordered to go towards the train station in Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thanks. You also mentioned in your statement that there was a check-point on the way to the station. Can you tell us who was manning this check-point that you saw?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: While we were going towards a train station, I was stopped two times at such check-points. Both times the people who were manning the check-points were Serb policemen. They asked for money, and they threatened us, that if they found money on us and we had not given it to them beforehand they would kill us. And they told us that, You have to go to Albania because you are asking for NATO.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kabashi, at page 5, in the last paragraph of your statement, you say that you stayed at the train station for three days and three nights. Can you describe what you saw there, at the train station, in those days.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I don't know if I'll be able to describe everything I saw, but what I saw during those three days and nights at the train station in Prishtina -- a normal person cannot even imagine that such things can happen to people. I saw thousands and thousands of people who were brought there from various neighbourhoods in Prishtina. They were loaded onto trains, both cargo trains and passenger trains. They were going -- the trains were going towards Macedonia because there is no other place to go. I -- the situation was very grave. I saw people dying, women giving birth in miserable conditions. I saw people who were sick with nobody to take care of them. I saw children crying all the time because of hunger. Everything you can see in a concentration camp where people have been displaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, when you took a train on the night of the third day, did you board that train voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I waited there for three days for my family members to come and join me because my family had gone to three different neighbourhoods in Prishtina, so that's why I was waiting there, for my family to come together with my mother. However, they did not come, so on the third day, early in the morning, the police came, and they took us to a waiting hall and forced us to get on to a freight train. It was very dirty. I don't know what was there, cement probably. And so we were told -- ordered to get on the train and the train started.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And after you boarded the train at the Pristina train station, can you tell us which route you travelled through from Pristina, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: The train from Prishtina follows this route: Fushe Kosove and the things we could see on -- from the train from the cracks on the doors and the walls of the carriages, we could see all the destruction and people that had been killed. So we went to Fushe Kosove, waited there for two or three hours; from there to Ferizaj; then to Elez Han, and there we were forced to get off the train and to work towards the border with Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kabashi, what happened when you arrived in Djeneral Jankovic before the border to Macedonia? You say you were told to get off the train. Where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: A little further from the train station at Elez Han, the train stopped and we were forced to get off, and we were told to walk between the rails, within the rails, because the area outside the rails was mined. We had to walk up to a point which is called Bllace. There police forces took the IDs from people, tore them up, threw them on the ground, and then allowed them to go by.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And can I ask you: Who told you to walk between the rails?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: The policemen because the train was escorted by policemen all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kabashi, can you describe how was the situation there in those days you spent in Bllace, Blace, what did you see there?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: What I saw there was terrible, something that resembles a situation that the people found themselves in during the Second World War in the concentration camps. There were thousands and thousands of people living out in the open without sufficient foodstuffs. I saw people digging graves for their dearest ones that had died near the banks of Lepenc river. Then I saw a man who came from Fushe Kosove who had been beaten and whom I knew from earlier. He died there. These images from Bllace cannot be described in words. People from this century can hardly imagine something like that happening in real terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kabashi, my last two questions. You were then eventually taken to Albania by bus. Do you remember roughly when that was?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Three days later, sometime between the 28th or 29th, or rather -- yes, that was the date in March -- I apologise. This must have been early April when an order was issued and a long column of buses -- in fact, we were assisted by a humanitarian organisation because my mother was ill and could not move. We left with this convoy of buses and one of the buses took us to Korca, a town in Albania, the following day.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thanks. So it was early April when you reached Albania?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thanks. My last question: Why did you and your family leave Kosovo, Mr. Kabashi? Did you leave voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: In war circumstances one cannot speak of voluntarily leaving your home, your country. Our house had been hit and burnt. We were forced to leave our house, to leave Kosova. We were forced to board cargo freight trains. We were forced to walk between this rail up to Bllace and to remain there in such conditions, because it was impossible to transport that many people under normal circumstances. This was a last exodus of last century of nation.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you very much for having answered my questions, Mr. Kabashi.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Djurdjic, do you cross-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kabashi, my name is Veljko Djurdjic. I'm a member of the Vlastimir Djordjevic Defence team and joined here today by Ms. Marie O'Leary, a member of my team. Our lead counsel is busy preparing our defence elsewhere and is therefore not here with us today, Mr. Dragoljub Djordjevic. Dr. Kabashi, in your statement dated the 24th of April, 1999, paragraph 2, you say that on the 25th of April [sic], 1999, there were eight persons in your house. Could you please list all the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: My mother; my brother, who happened to be there, he had come to visit our mother that was ill; his wife; my wife; my two nephews, my brother's son, my sister's son; and my elderly sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 2 you go on to state that among the police officers you recognised Simic and Pedza because they had interrogated you about the supply of food and medicine to the KLA back in 1998. What was the result of that interrogation?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I don't know what the result of that interrogation was. What I know is that I was kept for seven hours in the police station in Fushe Kosove. I knew these two persons. Simic was the commander of the police station while Pedza was the policeman who took me to the police station. Simic was also a neighbour of mine. His house was in my neighbourhood. They wanted to know what I was involved in, and I explained to them that I lived as every other ordinary citizen with no extraordinary activities involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please specify the period of 1998 in which this happened.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Sometime in September, late September/early October 1998. At around 4.00 a.m. I was getting ready for a journey; and as I was bringing back the car that was supposed to be brought back by my nephew, we were encircled and stopped by a police car. They ordered us to get off the car, to raise our hands up, and after that they took us to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 3 of the statement you state that at about 1500 hours, having received a telephone call, you sent eight members of your family to Pristina to two different homes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Not the eight members. What I said was the following. At the time when this bomb was thrown on my house, we were eight members of the family in the house; but during the same day I had sent my brother with his family and my wife to two different neighbourhoods in Prishtina. Because before that I had received two or three anonymous calls, threatening calls. Someone said that I should leave that place and go to Albania and similar things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Kabashi. I will read out the exact portion of your statement. This is paragraph 3, page 2. "On that day at about 1500 hours, I received an anonymous telephone call. The first two times there was no one on the other end of the line. When the phone rang for the third time I heard a male voice: 'You can expect NATO.' After these telephone calls, I sent eight members of my family to two different homes in different parts of Pristina ..."

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Part of my family because the eight of us remained there that night in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that the portion of the statement that I've read back to you is not accurate then?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No, this portion of the statement is correct. After I received this anonymous calls I sent the eight members of my family to two different houses in two different neighbourhoods in Prishtina, but other eight members of the family had remained in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, well a while ago you enumerated all the persons who were in your home and that added up to no more than eight persons. That was a while ago. When I asked you about who they were and you enumerated each and every one of them. Yet, now you tell us you sent eight of them away. How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: My youngest brother lived with me in the same house. It was a three-storey house. He was married. He had two children, so four together: My brother, his wife, and two children. Then my son, he was married, he had sons, so three others, total of seven. My daughter, one - eight. So these members were removed from the house after I received this threatening call and the other eight members that I mentioned to you earlier remained in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kabashi. But you've never said this before. You've never said before that there were 16 people there. I had asked you a while ago about who was in the house, and you said eight people, and you proceeded to give us their names. Now it seems there were a total of 16 people there. Never mind. Let us try and move on.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: When the bomb exploded in my house there were eight members of my house -- of my family in the house. There was no reason for me to give a higher or a lower number. This is the number of persons that were in the house when it was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kabashi. I'm asking questions, and you are doing your best to answer them. That's all. In paragraph 3 you go on to state that an hour later there was a power cut, soon after an explosion followed. Can you tell me who exactly was in the house at the time the explosion occurred?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Now, whether the electricity was cut off because of the explosion or because it was an ordinary occurrence during this time in Kosova, including Fushe Kosove and my house, at the time of the explosion, the bomb exploded in the corridor at the entrance of the room on the right side. We were three members of the family behind the door - we were seated, we were talking on the phone - my brother, my mother, and myself. In the other room were the remaining members of the family who were also sitting on the floor at the time of the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Kabashi, what about those rooms, were they facing the street or somewhere else? Could you tell us that, please.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: The windows of both rooms face the street in front of the house and the street on the side of the house. It's a one-way road, it's a small road, it's not a main road. So the front part of the house faces this road, while the other side of the house faces this other road here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there a wall separating the house from the street or road?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: At the time, there was no wall, but it was a kind of a fence, a fence encircling the yard of the house and separating the house from the street itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was that fence made of?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: The lower part just above the earth was of concrete and the other part was rails.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Imagine a person walking down that street, could they see from outside in the street exactly what was going on inside your house, looking in from outside, as it were?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: If the windows of the rooms facing the road are open or if the door leading to the corridor is open, they may well look inside the house from the street, the passers-by.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have the usual type of settee in your rooms?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: At the time of the event, it was the usual type of settee, kind of roundish, where usually my mother and myself and my brother would sit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps there is one thing that we ought to explain to the Chamber. That means that you didn't have any chairs in those rooms, did you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the other room, you said that you, your mother, and your brother were in one room. Who was in the other?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: My wife, my brother's wife, my older sister, and my oldest daughter were in the other room, and my daughter had a baby, a very small, young baby.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was your first reaction when the explosion occurred?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: When the explosion happened, I was speaking on the phone with someone. It was a land-line phone. I was behind the door, almost seated on the floor. When I heard the explosion, I told the members of my family who were with me in the room to lie down because they could get killed. The door fell on me and it probably was the door itself that saved my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What time was it when this happened?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: It was about 9.45 or 10.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right to say that the street lighting was off at the time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Not only at that time but there was never light on the streets, on those streets. There were no street lights.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Kabashi, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: From another room I saw those who had thrown the bomb and who had fired their weapons leaving the house. After some time, having realised that the bomb had destroyed everything in the corridor where it exploded, we carried my mother, who was ill, to a neighbour's house; and there we spent the night in a cellar, where we were more than 50 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Doctor. We'll be getting to that at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I request something if at all technically possible, and I think it should be. When the witness starts talking about something that is not related to my question or if he goes off on a tangent, there's nothing I can do in order to interrupt him and tell him that we might be getting back to that at a later stage because my microphone is off. Would it be possible for me to use my microphone and flick it on whenever I need to step in and direct the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness is not using the special voice-distortion microphone, so that you can have a microphone switched on at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm doing my best, but it's no use. I talk, I try to say something, but my voice is not taken up by the microphone and nothing is heard. That's why I'm asking. We could go through this a lot more quickly if only I were able to do that because the witness is providing some answers that are a little too extensive if anything. Thank you nonetheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, when you noticed those people leaving, can you describe exactly the scene that you saw.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Some of them I knew because they were my neighbours, those who were in civilians clothes. Some of them were policemen wearing police uniforms. I even knew some of the policemen from that group, they were neighbours of mine, and I knew them from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is precisely what I'm trying to ask you. It was pitch black outside and yet you were able to recognise quite a number of different persons; how come?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: The window from where I was looking out and the position from where the bomb was thrown and the gun-shots were fired was not more than 5 or 6 metres' distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Kabashi. Nevertheless, it was dark. You claim to have seem them leave, yet there was no lighting outside?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: The night of the 25th of March was not pitch black, as you describe it. You could still recognise silhouettes and bodies moving on the street, so I could see them leaving, withdrawing, from the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Kabashi. Could you perhaps help me with this: What was the name of the owner of the house to the cellar of which you took your mother, the distance between your house and that one being 200 metres, as you said?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: The owner of the house was Shemsedin Zogaj. They were my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on you said that you had gone to a three-storey-high house. Can you tell me where that house is, the one that you went to.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: It was in my neighbourhood and was the last house in the neighbourhood, about a hundred or so metres from my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the court transcriber to separate the last question from the last answer. As things stand now, it is all one thing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How far was that house from your house?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: A hundred or so metres away. I never measured the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I conclude that from that attic you were able to see your house?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before leaving Kosovo Polje, in paragraph 4 you say that you again came to your house. When was that, at what time and on what day?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: It was on the next day, on the 26th, early in the morning, maybe 7.00 a.m. When we saw that everything had been destroyed, I took the members of my family and left for Prishtina in my car.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where were your family members the night before?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: In the house where they had been sheltered, in Shemsedin Zogaj's cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say further on in this same paragraph that your brother counted 162 cases or cartridges in the house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: In the morning when we went back home, he collected that number of cartridges around the house and in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that you had heard three bursts of fire?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: At night when the house was fired at, after the explosion of the bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Dr. Kabashi, you did not eye-witness the killing of the 44 civilians of whom you speak in the paragraph 4 of your statement; am I right in claiming that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No, I did not see them. If I had seen them, I would testify to that effect in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Kabashi. Dr. Kabashi, in paragraph 5 you say that you went to Pristina and that you were accommodated in Dragodan, in Qemal Avdiu's house. As far as I understand, you were there with your wife and who else were there? It seems that I've forgotten. Who else was there of your family members?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: My brother with his wife and my daughter with her little baby, so two men and three women all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you confirmed that everybody in the house was Albanian. I would like to ask you this: The police officers came and they asked ID cards from all of the women; am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And they never made that same request upon the men?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Not at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in thinking that the police officers returned an ID to a woman?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. There was a woman there whom I didn't know who had taken shelter in the same house, and after they looked at her ID, they returned it to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Kabashi, am I right in thinking that the soldiers who were there wore blue camouflage uniforms, which were of a lighter shade than the police uniforms, and that they also wore masks on their faces?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No, the soldiers were not wearing masks, but the rest of it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are right, I misread your statement. The only thing that is mentioned are blue camouflage uniforms and I apologise. However, the soldiers bore the VJ insignia on their sleeves; am I right?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kabashi, am I right in thinking that you left Qamil Berisha's house and that you went to Rexhep Ajazi's house on your own. Nobody escorted you there, nobody made you go there?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: We went to Rexhep Ajazi's house after we were forced to leave Qamil's house. We stayed there for just one night. These houses were in the same neighbourhood but in different places in that neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, it was your choice to go to your friend's house, to your friend Rexhep's house?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: There was no other choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What I'm saying is this: It was not the police who took you to Rexhep's house; wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, that would be correct, but the police forced us out of Qamil Berisha's house, and in Rexhep Ajazi's house there were other people as well, not only my family and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 8 of your statement you say that on that day and during that night there was fighting in Vranjevac. Tell me, who was fighting whom?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I could not see who was fighting whom, but there were gun-shots, explosions. You could hear gun-fire, blasts, detonations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Kabashi, in your statement you also say that you knew two persons who were killed during that fighting?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, but the people who were killed, the fighting had occurred the night before and in another part of Vranjevc neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, it may be so, but I'm reading paragraph 8 in your statement and you also said that you had known the two men for 15 years?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kabashi, do you know that while you were in Vranjevac, the police station came under attack?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No, not when I was in Vranjevc, but when I was in Dragodan.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know whether this would be a good time for our first technical break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will have our first break now for the tapes to be rewound. We will resume again at 4.00. The court officer will show you out during the break, Mr. Kabashi, and we'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You told me that you'd been in Dragodan when the police station came under attack. From the place where you were, were you able to see that event?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, from there it's not more than 500 metres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that there was fighting around the houses that belonged to the Hartica family?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, the family's name is Hartica. A member of this family was a witness in this Tribunal. There was fighting there and there were killed people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that the police came during the fighting and after the fighting up to the place where you were at the time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: The police came after the fighting and told us to get out of Qamil Berisha's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that the police did not take any money from you on that occasion either?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: They asked for money, but I did not have much money. I just had 10 Deutschemarks, so they returned that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Kabashi, you said that a tank separated a column on the Vranjevac "most" and that they were divided into two groups. Could you please be more specific.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: At the time when the column I was part of reached that part of Prishtina, at the bridge - the bridge still exists today - there was a tank which divided the column in half; and part of the column went to the train station, and I was part of that same column. The other part went towards the Medrese neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was that tank on the bridge? In front of the bridge? Where was it?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: On the bridge, in the middle of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How come it was able to direct one group in the direction of the station and the other in the direction of the Medrese if you were all on the bridge?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: The people did not have any other way to go through. They had to pass the bridge, so there are two roads that lead from the bridge. One goes towards the train station and the other one goes towards the Medrese neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And each of you had a choice where to go, whether to go towards the train station or towards the Medrese?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. The police decided for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So this wouldn't have anything to do with the tank that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: It was related to the tank and the police that were there. A little further from the tank was the police check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the check-point that you have just mentioned, the police made checks pursuant to the list that was in their possession?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I saw the police list at the second check-point, not at the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Let's talk about the second check-point then. Why was your name on the list, Dr. Kabashi, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't know but I can assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the names of four of your friends were also on that list; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would you please be able to tell you [as interpreted] who they were?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: They were friends of mine. Among them was Dr. Flora Brovina; another comrade of mine, Nebi Bala; another young woman who was helping the cause of the war, Zahide Zeqiri; a young man Bajram Ruhani, who was also helping the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What would be your assumption as to why all of your names were on the list? Why were you on the list?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Maybe due to the fact that we were in middle of a war there, and they were active against those -- we were active against those who had caused the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was in Flora Brovina's house at the time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: It's not clear to me, your question. I don't know what was there in her house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As long as that means you don't know. Dr. Kabashi, you passed that check-point and the police didn't ID you.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: The police didn't ID me. They asked me for money. I showed them the 10 Deutschemarks I had on me, but I guess that was not enough for them, so they gave me that money back again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you get to see the list and your name on it? Where was the list?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: At the time when we were stopped by the police, one of the policemen asked for money, asked us to produce money; and as I was taking the money out of my pocket, he took out a list with typed names, the names that I mentioned, typed on computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were the police escorting you as you were moving towards the railway station in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: On both sides of the road there were policemen escorting the column and there were also policemen on the check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where was the house whose owner had opened a door and invited you inside?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: This house was some 200 metres before the second check-point that we mentioned. This was a small road leading to the main road. A person whom I knew opened the door to his house and invited us in, but I refused to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How far were you from where the person was standing who invited you in?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Maybe some 10 metres far.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When he opened the door and invited you in, he wasn't fired at, was he?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No, not at that particular moment because the check-point, the police check-point, was about 100 or 200 metres away from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. He wasn't scared of just opening that door and inviting you inside, was he?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: That I don't know. I didn't have the time and the opportunity to ask him whether he was scared or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Kabashi, is my understanding correct that you remained for three days at the railway station in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And is my understanding correct that you remained out in the open for three days without a roof over your head?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Three days and three nights, thousands and thousands of people remained outside in the open.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have a telephone on you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No, at that time there were no mobile phones.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You remained at the station waiting for your family to arrive; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Over those three days, no one forced you to get onto the train, did they?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: When the trains would arrive, we would avoid boarding them. There were many people there to board those trains.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The fact is you spent three days there waiting for your family to arrive; right?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You then took a train to Djeneral Jankovic and then you spent another six days at Djeneral Jankovic waiting for your family to arrive; right?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where were you staying throughout all this time while you were waiting for your family at Djeneral Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: We were forced to remain at the location called Bllace.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, Blace is in which country exactly?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: It belongs to Macedonia currently.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Blace was always in what used to be then the Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Not always.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, when did Blace become part of what is now the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: After Serbia --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Kosova became part of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And which year was that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: After 1913.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you about Djeneral Jankovic. You're waiting for your family. Where are you staying, and this is before you left for Blace.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: We were not staying at the train station at Hani i Elezit. The train proceeded to the border and some 2 or 3 kilometres before the border the train stopped. We were forced to get off and to walk between the tracks, to cross the border with Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Kabashi, is it not true that for the first six nights of NATO air-strikes not a single Albanian accessed the shelter?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I don't know for other Albanians. As for me and members of my family, as early as during the first night, we had to leave our house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kabashi, my question was: Was it not true for the first six nights of NATO air-strikes not a single Albanian accessed the shelter?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I am not clear about the shelter you mentioned. What kind of shelter do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kabashi, any shelter that a person might come across in a bid to protect themselves from the air-strikes. I'm just reading paragraph 16 of your own statement. "During the first six nights of NATO air-strikes, not a single Albanian accessed the shelter or took shelter, generally speaking."

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: This is correct. This is the period that I remained there for, and I didn't see people, Albanians I mean, going into shelters because of NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How could you see them going to shelters?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I lived there. Until the 24th I moved about in different parts of Kosova. On the 24th of March, when I came back, I saw my neighbours, people from my hometown, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I was asking about how you knew during the actual air-strike that people were not seeking shelter or going into shelters?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I knew this because I met these people, I saw these people, and as I was not seeking shelter they were not seeking shelter either.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have document OTP 65 ter list 00013.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kabashi, could you please draw on the map the building of the district court in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: To what I can see on the map, because there are no markings, it should be in this black square with the red dot in it or in that area more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you kindly circle the place where the district court was approximately. I know that you can't do it exactly.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: If the location just above it is the stadium of Prishtina, this here in the middle should be the building that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please put a number 1 next to that, sir.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please mark the location of the Pristina SUP building.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: This is the building, both that of the court and of the SUP. The annexed here building on the right is a court building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kabashi, what about the district court and the SUP, aren't they both in the main street crossing Pristina?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: The district court building is on another location in Prishtina, whereas the court -- I don't know what it's called, misdemeanour court or something like that, was in another location, and it shared the building with the secretariat of internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, what about the location you marked, is that the misdemeanours court or the district court?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: This is the building of the misdemeanour court as far as I know, not the district court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I think so too, Dr. Kabashi. That's why I asked you about the location of the district court in Pristina because that is the one you mention in your statement.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: It is very difficult for me to orient myself on this map. The district court of Prishtina is on the road leading to Podujeve, on the right-hand side of that road. If this right -- red line is a road going to Podujeve, or as it is called now Besiana, the district court building should be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I think so too, Dr. Kabashi. Nevertheless, could you please proceed and mark the location of the district court. You claim that you saw the main road?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I don't know how precise or detailed this map is, but just for orientation, the district court building should be here, the circle that I just marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Kabashi. I think you marked it well. What about the post office, the post office building, could you mark that too please.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: If the centre were marked, the post office building would have been here. I just made a small circle there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Kabashi. Could you please put a number 3 there.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you please make it a little more visible. We can't make out the actual number.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And right next to the district court building, put a number 2. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Kabashi, do you know that these buildings were bombed by NATO?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No. The district court building was not bombed; however, the building of the SUP and the post office building were bombed. I did not see the bombing of the post office building because I was not in Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about the district court?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I was in Dragodan that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Aren't both buildings, the district court and the SUP, right in the centre of Pristina?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No, the district court building is not in the centre of Prishtina; it's on the road to Podujeve, as I explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Fine, Dr. Kabashi. You say that when that residential building that was targeted, when the other two --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could counsel please be asked to re-ask the question. The interpreter did not understand the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you mind repeating that question, please, Mr. Djurdjic; it could not be picked up properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Indeed I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kabashi, when the Pristina SUP building was targeted and when the Belgrade district court was targeted, what about the residential buildings surrounding those two buildings, were they not targeted and destroyed as well?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Kabashi. I looked at your statement, and I conclude that while you were on your way to the railway station in Pristina and then from there to Djeneral Jankovic, you were out in the open all this time, were you not, unsheltered; am I right to say that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were you receiving any information throughout that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No, I couldn't get any information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How then were you able to say in your statement that you had no information coming from the Serbian authorities, television, or any other media as to what exactly was going on?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: From the time I reached the station and onwards, but up to the time I went to the station, I did have some information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Nevertheless, you told us that the electricity was out?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Well, the power was not cut off all the time, non-stop, it would be on some of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kabashi, you made your first statement in April 1999, then you appeared in the Milosevic trial. Between these two statements you said that you had seen Frenki's and Arkan's men in Pristina -- or rather, the first time you said that was while testifying in the Milutinovic trial. Can you explain how this came about, you suddenly remembering that on the 21st of August, 2006, which is the date of your evidence in the Milutinovic trial?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Because the accused, Milosevic, did not ask me about that before, and I did not have any reason to answer a question that was not asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Indeed, Dr. Kabashi. But back in 1999 an investigator of this Tribunal spoke to you and also the Prosecutor in the Milutinovic trial, who was the person asking you questions, and in the Milosevic trial too. It wasn't just Mr. Milosevic. I do apologise, but you didn't say that, did you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Because they did not ask me these questions, and I didn't think that I had to answer them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in thinking that you remained the -- a member of the KLA on the 28th November 2000 -- 1997?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to correct something in the transcript. I can see the year 2000 first and then 1997. I'm wondering whether my question was clear or should I maybe repeat it and correct the transcript accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please make clear what it is that you're -- which year you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kabashi, is it true that you became a member of the KLA on the 28th November 1997?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that you and some other colleagues of yours performed some duties for the KLA wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that women and young girls were also members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in thinking that some of them wore uniforms and arms and that some of them wore civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that you were a member of a unit or a KLA formation based in Pristina which was responsible for the guerilla activities that took place in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kabashi, could you please tell me about the basis of the subgroups of the KLA in Pristina, where were those located?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: They were located in several parts of Prishtina. Some of them I knew about, some of them I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that they were also at a clinic run by Dr. Brovina?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: That was one of the main bases. It was a clinic, an out-patient centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that you carried arms when you went on field missions?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, every time I went on field missions I did carry a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, you did not have a licence to carry arms; am I right?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: You're right, but I did not have -- where to get it from, that kind of licence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your activity in the KLA and the fact that you carried arms were the reasons why you were taken into custody in September 1997, that you were brought in to the police station in Kosovo Polje?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Not in 1997 but in 1998, and if those were the reasons why, I would not be here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you explain, how come you wouldn't be here, if you know?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: That was a war and a war is conducted between two enemy sides, and when these enemies meet they kill each other. That's the logic of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Kabashi. We're talking about September 1998 and you are alive, thankfully. In the statement you provided on the 24th of April, 1999, in paragraph 2 thereof you say about that event, about you being brought to the police, that you had been accused of providing the KLA with food and medicines, which means that the police were aware of that activity of yours.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: The police were making assumptions. If they were sure about it, they wouldn't discuss those things with me at all. Secondly, the police did not have any facts or evidence about my activities. Thirdly, I did not admit to anything that the police put to me, and that's why I think I was released with two other members of my family, my son and my nephew.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Kabashi, at the Milosevic trial you said that you had two sons and a daughter, and it seems to me that earlier today you said you had two daughters and a son. Which of the two is correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I was not here today in the morning, but when I was asked I said a boy and two girls, so a son and two daughters, three children all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Today for the first time you said that during the relevant time, during May of 1999, one of your daughters had a baby. You'd never mentioned that before in any of your statements, at any of the trials? How come that you remember that for the first time earlier today and only then?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can I please have a reference for that. It's not my recollection that the witness said that his daughter had a baby.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me reply, my learned friend. Maybe an hour ago the witness said that a daughter of his had a baby at the time and that she was with them in the house, either in Vranjevc or Dragodan. I believe that the witness can either confirm that or say that I'm not right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you have the transcript reference there, Mr. Djurdjic? Could you give that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, but I would like the witness to confirm or deny. This is page 18, line 19, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. That is consistent with the recollection of the Chamber as well, Ms. D'Ascoli. Carry on, please, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kabashi, you heard my question or should I repeat it? Let me repeat. You said that in March 1999 your daughter had a small baby and you said -- you mentioned that for the first time today.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, my daughter had given birth earlier, she was married, had a child, and it is together with that child that she left Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, you did not mention that fact in any of your statements. It was only today that this came up.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I didn't think it was relevant, and maybe those people who asked me questions so far did not think it was relevant either.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kabashi, nobody asked you that today. My learned friend did not even remember you mentioning the fact and wanted me to remind her of where this came up.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Maybe she really didn't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kabashi, am I right in saying that in 1974 you were also arrested?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why? What were the reasons?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: The indictment said for hostile activities against the people and the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If there were proceedings instituted against you, could you tell us what the outcome of that was?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I was kept in prison for eight months, and then the court decided to stop me from carrying out my education activities and my publishing activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Am I right in saying that from 1974 to 1992 you worked in an iron alloys factory?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Feronikel, yes, but that was from 1976. Till 1976 I was unemployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I've taken the date from the Milutinovic trial -- I apologise, the Milosevic trial. Is it correct that during the relevant time, i.e., 1974, Albanians were in high positions, both in Kosovo and in the Federation?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. They were members of the Yugoslav Presidency as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right, Dr. Kabashi, in saying you were also taken in custody in 1968?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you were also arrested in 1981 for your participation in demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1981 the demonstrations were organised by students, those were students demonstrations; am I right?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: They were student demonstrations, but also other sections of the population participated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time the slogan "Kosovo Republic" was the first time heard. Can you please explain the meaning of that slogan?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: The demand for Kosova to be a republic was proclaimed, first in 1968 and then repeated in 1981. The meaning of the slogan was -- at that time the movement in Kosova did not demand the destruction of Yugoslavia but just was asking for equal rights to other peoples of Yugoslavia. That is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that that meant that Kosovo was to be given the status of a republic, and it would no longer be part of the Republic of Serbia; was that the demand?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Well, if it became a republic it couldn't be part of the Republic of Serbia anymore, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that in 1989 you were also arrested?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that your position was that the only way to become free is to win freedom by means of arms?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I thought, what I said, and what I wrote publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that after 1989 you tried to explain to other people that the only thing that could bring freedom was to -- for people to start on a war path?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No, not in 1989. I explained this to my students in 1974, and that's why I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you say that you started spreading that idea as of 1974?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I don't know if I was spreading that idea, but I know that I did say that to my students because I felt it was my moral obligation to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that you supported NATO campaigns against the SR Yugoslavia because that should have protected people who pursuant to the plan of the Serbian academy would have been resettled and broken up as a nation?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: It is true that I supported the NATO campaign; however, the second part of your question remains unclear to me, when you mention the Serbian Academy of Science.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kabashi, this is a quote from the Milosevic trial. The second part of your answer referred to your support to the NATO aggression because NATO should have protected the people who would have been resettled and broken up as a nation according to the Serbian academy plan, and you will find that on page 4036 on lines between 18 and 25.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: The part referring to NATO is correct; however, the part pertaining to the academy, you're either misreading it or I'm not understanding it properly. But I can repeat the same answer that I gave Milosevic at that trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let me try and jog your memory. You even said that it was an academy document and you mentioned the name of Mr. Vladan Djordjevic. I don't know whether this jogs your memory in any way.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: My memory serves me very well, but I did not mention these details in the context that you are putting me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce D002-1922 -- but before that, Your Honour, if I could -- thank you. Could I tender into evidence the plan of the city of Pristina where the witness marked a few locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D00054, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce page - and I'm checking the number, if you can please bear with me - 4018 is the page number, this is 4008, and I've asked for 4018. Lines 17, 18, 19 -- I apologise, I got my pages mixed up. The page number is 4036. I apologise. From line 18 through 20, where possible 25 even. Could I please be shown the page number on the screen. 4036, I am looking for line 18, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kabashi, do I have to read the text for you, or do you perhaps understand what it says in these lines, from 18 through 22?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I have the English version before me, not the Albanian one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'll try to read it for you then. [In English] "I supported and approved the NATO actions because it was taking under protection a people that, on the basis of the plans of the Serb academy, was meant to be displaced and dismembered as a people."

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you mention the Serbian academy?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I did mention the Serbian academy in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 4037, please, page 4037, lines 8 and 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Line 8 says: [In English] "It is a document of 1884, until the one that you have implemented. One of Vladan Djordjevic."

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: That's correct. This is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Dr. Kabashi, what was the objective of the KLA after the beginning of NATO air-strikes?
